title: the first symbol of the scripture
hook: the first symbol of the scripture — one

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanak, the boy who asked what the thread was for. Your line was there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Did you catch yourself seeing a label before a person? Day four.

Open almost any book and the first thing you see is a title, or a name, or once upon a time. Open the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, fourteen hundred pages of hymns, and the very first thing on the very first page isn't a word at all. It's a symbol. You may have seen it without knowing: on a gold pendant, on a car's dashboard, painted over a shop door, tattooed on a forearm. It looks a little like the number one with a sweeping curve flying off it. Guru Nanak put it at the head of everything. Before any story, before any rule, before any song: this. Today, the first symbol.
screen: `FOURTEEN HUNDRED PAGES.` → `THE FIRST THING ISN'T A WORD.` → `IT'S A SYMBOL.`

segments.voice: It's called Ik Onkar. Look closely at how it's written. It starts with a numeral: the digit one. Not the word one. The number, the one you'd write on a price tag. That's Ik. Then comes Onkar, a very old sound for the divine, related to Om, the sacred syllable many of Nanak's neighbors already chanted. And then that curve, sweeping up and out, which many Sikhs read as a line with no end. Put it together and it says: there is one. One God, one reality, one source behind everything. So why a number instead of a word? Here's what Sikh teachers often point out. A word can be argued with. A word belongs to one language, one people. But a numeral is the plainest thing there is. Everyone agrees on one. Nanak seems to have chosen the least arguable mark possible to open his scripture. And notice what that one includes. On this path, the one God isn't somewhere far away looking down on creation. The hymns say the one is in everything, the whole of it: in you, in the person across the street, in the river and the dust. So if there's one, then nobody is outside it. You can hear yesterday's line underneath: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. If there's one, the labels come second. Ik Onkar is also a promise about the rest of the book. Everything that follows, all fourteen hundred pages, is an unfolding of this first mark. Tomorrow we'll read the line that comes right after it. Today, just the one.
screen: `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · `ONKAR — AN ANCIENT SOUND FOR GOD.` · `A NUMBER NOBODY CAN ARGUE WITH.` · `IF THERE'S ONE, NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `THERE IS ONE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, notice yourself: your hands, your chest rising. On the second, notice something beyond you: a sound in the room, a person you love. On the third, hold both at once, and let the word ride out on the breath if you like: one.
Ik Onkar. The numeral one, with an ancient sound for God. There is one, and it opens the whole scripture. Fourth word.
Your line: one. Today, when someone annoys you, try thinking it just once: same source. See what it does. Day four.

screen: `DAY 4 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "ONE CREATOR, TRUTH IS THE NAME."`

howItsDone: Ik Onkar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and begins the Mool Mantar, which Sikhs recite daily; the symbol is written, painted and worn as a reminder of the one God.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the numeral one (੧) joined to the letter for Onkar, with its open curve; one symbol, one character.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty religious symbol.
what it means: there is one: one God, one source, in everything, so no one stands outside it.
what a scholar hears: it's a numeral, not a word, fused with Onkar, a form related to Om. Sikh commentators stress the numeral: one, without a second.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Ik Onkar at the head of the Mool Mantar)
Guru Granth Sahib, passim (the one God present in all)

notes: Onkar described as 'related to Om'; some Sikh commentators resist linking it to Om. Confirm the phrasing.
The curve read as 'a line with no end' is a common devotional reading, framed as 'many Sikhs read'. Confirm.
Pronunciation of ੴ varies (ik oankar, ik onkar, ek oangkar). Confirm the guide.
'Fourteen hundred pages' refers to the standard 1,430 Angs.
